questions.question: Explain, with verbal diagrams, how a maximum price and a minimum price each disturb a market, and evaluate the minimum wage from both sides.
questions.expected_answer: A maximum price — the ceiling — binds only when set below equilibrium: at the ceiling, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, opening a permanent shortage whose consequences follow mechanically — queues, rationing and black markets where the good resells above the legal price. A minimum price — the floor — binds only above equilibrium: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a permanent surplus the state must buy up, store or export at a budget cost. The minimum wage is a floor in the labour market: it raises the incomes of workers who keep their jobs and protects against exploitation, but at a wage above equilibrium the quantity of labour demanded can fall, so the policy trades higher pay for some against fewer posts for others — a complete answer states both halves.

questions.question: Trace the evolution of markets from self-sufficiency to industrial development, naming the problem each stage solved.
questions.expected_answer: Self-sufficiency: households produce all they consume — no surplus, no trade. Surplus and barter: better tools create extras to swap, but barter is braked by the double coincidence of wants — each trader must find someone who has what they want and wants what they have. Money releases the brake through four functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, and standard of deferred payment — widening markets from village to world. Governments then enter to issue and protect currency, enforce contracts, regulate quality, tax trade and provide roads, courts and schooling. Finally industrial development: machines, factories and wage labour multiply production and pull people to towns — in South Africa through the mineral revolution, with diamonds and gold drawing railways, capital and migrant labour inland.

questions.question: Diagnose the five types of unemployment from scenarios and explain how economic redress works through the four factors of production.
questions.expected_answer: Frictional: between jobs, needing faster matching and information. Structural: skills or location mismatched to employers' needs — South Africa's dominant type — needing education, training and spatial remedies. Cyclical: retrenchments in a downswing, needing demand. Seasonal: harvest or holiday work, needing diversification and off-season options. Technological: machines replacing tasks, needing retraining toward what machines cannot do. Redress organises by factor: land — restitution, redistribution, secure tenure; labour — employment equity and skills development; capital — broad-based ownership, preferential procurement, access to finance; entrepreneurship — small-business support. The evaluation point: instruments need partners — a title deed without seed money, a learnership without a job, a tender without working capital each falls short — and decisions are democratised through unions, public hearings and NEDLAC seating government, business, labour and community.
